country.name: Armenia
country.tagline: Home of the world's oldest known winery, Urartian cellars of buried karas jars and a mountain wine revival around Areni.

stats.note: Wine-grape area roughly 15,000 to 17,000 ha in the 2020s (most grapes historically went to brandy); production figures vary by source and are not reported by OIV 2025.

country.overview:
In 2007 archaeologists digging in a three-chambered limestone cave above the Arpa river, near the village of Areni in Vayots Dzor, found a winery: a clay basin about a metre long for treading grapes, sloping to drain juice into a vat about 60 centimetres deep, storage jars, cups, grape seeds, pressed skins and vines, all preserved by the cave's dry air and a layer of sheep dung. Radiocarbon dating placed it around 4100 to 4000 BC, and a 2011 paper by Hans Barnard and colleagues in the Journal of Archaeological Science confirmed malvidin, the pigment of red grapes, in the vessels. Areni-1 is the oldest winery yet found, and the same cave gave the world's oldest leather shoe.

Wine runs through the Urartian kingdom that ruled the Armenian Highlands in the first millennium BC. At Teishebaini (Karmir Blur), a fortress built by King Rusa II on the edge of today's Yerevan, excavators found storerooms with hundreds of karases, huge clay jars sunk into the ground, with capacity marks on their shoulders. Xenophon's Greek army, marching through in 401 BC, was served wine and beer from jars buried in village houses.

Christianity, adopted in 301, kept wine sacred; cross-stones (khachkars) are carved with vines and pomegranates. In the Soviet era Armenia's grapes went mostly into brandy: the Yerevan brandy distillery (founded in 1887, bought by Nikolay Shustov's company in 1899, famous as Ararat brandy and owned by Pernod Ricard since 1998) supplied a quarter of all Soviet brandy, and wine was largely sherry-style or bulk. Since about 2010 a wine renaissance has followed: Zorah (Rind), Trinity Canyon, Old Bridge, Hin Areni, Momik, Voskevaz, ArmAs, Van Ardi, Keush (sparkling at 1,750 metres) and many small producers now bottle native grapes from some of the highest vineyards in the northern hemisphere.

The signature grapes are the red Areni Noir (Areni), thick-skinned, peppery and fresh, grown on its own roots in Vayots Dzor's sandy, volcanic soils at 1,000 to 1,600 metres, and the white Voskehat ('golden berry'), floral and textured. Kangun, a Soviet-era cross, and the red Haghtanak and Sireni (Khndoghni) are also important. The traditional vessel, the karas, is being revived by producers who ferment and age in clay. The Areni Wine Festival, held each October since 2009, celebrates the village's double legacy.

history.title: The Areni-1 winery
history.text: A cave near Areni held a clay treading basin, a fermentation vat, storage jars and domesticated grape remains: the oldest winery yet discovered (Barnard et al. 2011).

history.title: The Areni-1 shoe
history.text: The same cave preserved the world's oldest known leather shoe, found in 2008.

history.title: Erebuni founded
history.text: The Urartian king Argishti I founded the fortress of Erebuni, origin of Yerevan, whose storerooms held wine jars.

history.title: Teishebaini's wine magazines
history.text: Rusa II's fortress at Karmir Blur had storerooms of buried karases; excavations from 1939 found hundreds of jars, many with capacity marks, before its destruction around 585 BC.

history.title: Xenophon's buried jars
history.text: Xenophon's Anabasis describes Armenian villagers storing wine and barley beer in jars sunk into the floors of their houses.

history.title: The Yerevan brandy distillery
history.text: The first brandy factory opened in Yerevan; after Nikolay Shustov's company bought it in 1899 it made Armenian brandy famous across the Russian Empire.

history.title: Excavation and publication of Areni-1
history.text: An Armenian, Irish and American team excavated the cave from 2007; the winery was announced in January 2011.

country.classification: Armenia has no EU-style appellation system yet. Labels carry the region (Vayots Dzor, Ararat Valley, Aragatsotn, Armavir, Tavush) and the grape; the Vine and Wine Foundation of Armenia promotes the sector, and 'Armenian brandy' is a protected name.
country.climate_soils: Dry, sunny, continental highland climate with hot summers, very cold winters and big day-night swings; vineyards range from about 800 metres in the Ararat Valley to over 1,700 metres. Soils are volcanic (basalt, tuff), sandy and stony, which kept phylloxera out of much of Vayots Dzor, so many old vines are ungrafted.

grapes.name: Areni Noir
grapes.note: The great native red: medium-bodied, peppery, sour cherry and violet, often ungrafted at high altitude.

grapes.name: Voskehat
grapes.note: The leading native white, floral, apricot and honey.

grapes.name: Kangun
grapes.note: Soviet-era white cross (Rkatsiteli by Sukholimansky), used for wine and brandy.

grapes.name: Haghtanak
grapes.note: Deep-coloured red cross used in blends and dessert wines.

grapes.name: Sireni (Khndoghni)
grapes.note: Red of the Karabakh/Artsakh area, dark and tannic.

grapes.name: Garan Dmak, Chilar, Mskhali, Lalvari, Kakhet

further_reading: The Wines of Armenia (Vine and Wine Foundation of Armenia)

sources.title: Barnard, H. et al. (2011), Chemical evidence for wine production around 4000 BCE in the Late Chalcolithic Near Eastern highlands, Journal of Archaeological Science 38(5)

regions.name: Vayots Dzor
regions.tagline: The gorge of the Arpa: Areni Noir, karas and the oldest winery on earth.
regions.summary: Armenia's most celebrated wine region follows the Arpa river through red-rock gorges from Areni to Yeghegnadzor and beyond. Vineyards at 1,000 to 1,600 metres grow ungrafted Areni Noir; the Areni-1 cave and the Noravank monastery are next to the vines. Zorah at Rind, Trinity Canyon and Hin Areni are the best-known estates.
regions.history: Areni-1 winery (about 4100 BC); medieval monasteries such as Noravank (thirteenth century); Soviet-era Areni wine factory.
regions.terroir: Very dry, sunny, high; volcanic and sandy limestone soils, cold winters.
regions.styles: Fresh, peppery reds; whites; karas-aged wines.

sources.title: Barnard, H. et al. (2011), Chemical evidence for wine production around 4000 BCE in the Late Chalcolithic Near Eastern highlands, Journal of Archaeological Science 38(5)

regions.name: Ararat Valley
regions.tagline: The hot plain beneath Mount Ararat, historic home of brandy grapes.
regions.summary: The broad valley of the Araks south and west of Yerevan, at 800 to 1,000 metres, with Mount Ararat across the Turkish border. It supplies most of the grapes for Armenian brandy and many table grapes; Urartian Teishebaini and Erebuni were wine centres. Armavir to the west and parts of Ararat province are covered.
regions.history: Urartian fortresses with wine magazines; Soviet brandy factories.
regions.terroir: Hot summers, irrigation, alluvial and volcanic soils.

sources.title: Barnard, H. et al. (2011), Chemical evidence for wine production around 4000 BCE in the Late Chalcolithic Near Eastern highlands, Journal of Archaeological Science 38(5)

regions.name: Aragatsotn
regions.tagline: Mount Aragats' southern slopes: Voskehat and the Ashtarak sherry tradition.
regions.summary: Vineyards on the slopes south of Mount Aragats around Ashtarak, Voskevaz and Oshakan grow Voskehat and other whites; Soviet oenologists developed Armenian flor 'sherry' here in the 1930s. Voskevaz winery and ArmAs are the leading producers.
regions.history: Karases dating to the seventh century were found at the church of Surp Hovhannes in Voskevaz.

sources.title: Barnard, H. et al. (2011), Chemical evidence for wine production around 4000 BCE in the Late Chalcolithic Near Eastern highlands, Journal of Archaeological Science 38(5)

regions.name: Tavush
regions.summary: The northern province bordering Georgia and Azerbaijan, around Ijevan and Berd, has a more humid climate, forests and a Soviet-era winery at Ijevan; small producers are reviving it.
regions.history: A Soviet-era state winery at Ijevan anchored the region.
regions.terroir: Lower altitude (500 to 900 metres), more rain.

sources.title: Barnard, H. et al. (2011), Chemical evidence for wine production around 4000 BCE in the Late Chalcolithic Near Eastern highlands, Journal of Archaeological Science 38(5)

sites.name: Areni-1 cave winery
sites.text: A three-chambered karst cave above the Arpa river where a winery of about 4100 to 4000 BC was excavated from 2007: a clay basin for treading grapes, a 60-centimetre vat, storage jars, cups and domesticated grape remains, with malvidin residues confirmed in 2011. The cave also yielded the world's oldest leather shoe (about 3500 BC).

sites.name: Teishebaini (Karmir Blur)
sites.text: Urartian fortress of King Rusa II, built in the seventh century BC on the Red Hill at the edge of Yerevan and burnt around 585 BC. Its storerooms were lined with rows of karases, giant clay jars sunk into the floor and marked with their capacity; excavations from 1939 to 1971 recovered hundreds of them.

sites.name: Erebuni Fortress
sites.text: The fortress founded by the Urartian king Argishti I in 782 BC, origin of Yerevan; its storerooms included wine jars, and a museum displays karases.

sites.name: Noravank Monastery
sites.text: Thirteenth-century monastery in a red-rock gorge near Areni, with carved grapevines on its churches, at the heart of Vayots Dzor wine country.

sites.name: Zorah Wines, Rind
sites.text: Founded by Zorik Gharibian, an Armenian-Italian fashion entrepreneur, with vineyards of ungrafted Areni at about 1,400 metres in Rind; its Karasì red, aged in karases, helped put Armenian wine on the world map.

sites.name: Trinity Canyon Vineyards
sites.text: A pioneering estate at Aghavnadzor in Vayots Dzor, making Areni, Voskehat and karas-aged wines at about 1,400 metres.

sites.name: Voskevaz Winery
sites.text: Historic winery in Voskevaz on Aragats' southern slopes, founded in 1932, which revived karas winemaking.

sites.name: ArmAs
sites.text: Estate at Nor Yedesia in Aragatsotn with one of Armenia's largest modern vineyards and a winery making native and international varieties.

sites.name: Yerevan Brandy Company (Ararat)
sites.text: The brandy house founded in 1887 and bought by Nikolay Shustov's company in 1899, maker of Ararat brandy; owned by Pernod Ricard since 1998. Its cellars by the Hrazdan river hold barrels laid down for famous visitors.
